name: Handing Regulation Back to Students
title: Handing Regulation Back to Students
answer: Handing regulation back to students means deliberately shifting control of learning decisions, such as goal setting, practice choice and progress checking, from the adaptive system and teacher to the student over time. It matters because a student who never makes those choices never learns how to manage their own learning, and the aim is a learner who can work well without the system.

sections.body: Adaptive systems often make learning decisions on the student's behalf, deciding what to practice, when to move on and how long to spend. This can produce short term gains while leaving students unable to direct their own learning. The proposed response is hybrid human and AI regulation, in which the system and teacher initially guide most of the student's learning and then gradually release decisions to the student. The decisions being handed over include setting goals, choosing practice and checking progress. The intended outcome is a student who can learn well independently of the system.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Teachers can plan the handoff across the school year rather than leaving it to chance. Early in the year the teacher and the software set goals for students, by midyear students set their own goals with guidance, and by the end of the year they set and track goals independently. Goal tracking features found in many platforms can support this shift. Throughout, the teacher watches for signs that students are growing more capable rather than more dependent. The approach is described for learners aged 10 to 14.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea as coming from research, citing a proposal by Molenaar in 2022 for hybrid human and AI regulation for learners aged 10 to 14. The proposal describes an initial stage where the system and teacher guide much of the learning, followed by a gradual handoff of decisions such as goal setting, practice choice and progress checking back to the student. No study results, sample sizes or outcome figures are given in the supplied text, so the evidence rests on the proposed approach rather than reported findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk is that adaptive systems quietly take over decisions students need to learn to make, which can help in the short term but leave students unable to manage their own learning. The handoff must therefore be gradual and monitored, with the teacher checking that students are becoming more capable rather than more dependent. Decisions about when and how much control to release stay with the teacher, and the goal remains a student who can learn well without the system. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
